heading: RBI FCNR(B) Big Bang: How NRIs Can Now Earn Up to 7.4% on Dollar Deposits With Zero Currency Risk
story:
RBI FCNR(B) Big Bang: How NRIs Can Now Earn Up to 7.4% on Dollar Deposits With Zero Currency Risk

Mumbai, June 21, 2026 -- The Reserve Bank of India has pulled out its biggest weapon to attract foreign currency into the country. In a series of moves announced between June 5 and June 17, 2026, the RBI has temporarily removed interest rate caps on FCNR(B) deposits, introduced a special US Dollar-Rupee forex swap facility with zero hedging costs, and opened the door for NRIs to earn up to 7.4 per cent on dollar fixed deposits -- all without taking any currency risk. For the estimated 13.5 million Non-Resident Indians worldwide, this could be the most attractive opportunity in years to park their foreign earnings in India. But what exactly is happening, why is the RBI doing this, and should you act on it? Here is everything you need to know.

What is FCNR(B)? A Simple Explanation

FCNR(B) stands for Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank). It is a type of fixed deposit account that Indian banks offer specifically to Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) and Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs). The key feature: you deposit money in a foreign currency -- US Dollars, British Pounds, Euros, Japanese Yen, and others -- and you earn interest in that same currency. When the deposit matures, you get your principal and interest back in the foreign currency. You never have to convert to rupees if you do not want to.

This is fundamentally different from an NRE (Non-Resident External) deposit, where you bring foreign currency but it gets converted to rupees, and an NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account, which holds your India-sourced income in rupees. In an FCNR(B) deposit, your money stays in foreign currency from start to finish.

Think of it this way: if you are an Indian working in Dubai earning Dirhams, or a software engineer in Silicon Valley earning US Dollars, you can open an FCNR(B) deposit in an Indian bank, park your dollars there for 1 to 5 years, earn interest in dollars, and when the term ends, take your dollars back. No currency conversion, no exchange rate risk.

What Changed? The RBI June 2026 Bombshell

On June 5, 2026, the RBI announced a US Dollar-Rupee Forex Swap Facility for fresh FCNR(B) deposits. Then on June 17, it went further -- temporarily removing the interest rate ceiling on both FCNR(B) and NRE deposits until September 30, 2026. These are not small tweaks. They represent the most significant liberalisation of NRI deposit rules since the 2013 taper-tantrum era.

Here is what the RBI did, broken down simply:

1. Zero Hedging Cost on FCNR(B) Deposits

Normally, when a bank takes in dollars through an FCNR(B) deposit, it faces a currency risk. The bank needs rupees to lend in India, but it has dollars. So it does a swap with the RBI -- handing over dollars and getting rupees at today's exchange rate, with an agreement to reverse the transaction at the same rate when the deposit matures. The cost of this protection is called the hedging cost, and it is typically around 3.5 per cent per year. Under the new scheme, the RBI is absorbing this cost entirely for FCNR(B) deposits mobilised until September 30, 2026. Banks pay zero hedging cost.

2. Interest Rate Caps Removed Until September 30

Until June 17, banks were not allowed to offer more than a certain interest rate on FCNR(B) deposits -- the cap was linked to international benchmark rates plus a small spread. The RBI has now removed this cap entirely, at least until September 30, 2026. This means banks can now compete freely for NRI dollars by offering whatever rate the market will bear.

3. CRR and SLR Exemptions

FCNR(B) deposits mobilised under this special window are exempt from Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements. Normally, banks must park a portion of every deposit with the RBI as reserves, which reduces their ability to lend and earn. With this exemption, banks can lend out the full amount, making FCNR(B) deposits far more profitable for them -- and allowing them to offer higher rates to depositors.

4. Daily Reporting Mandate

The RBI has asked all banks to report their FCNR(B) mobilisation on a daily basis. This is to closely monitor the inflows and ensure the measures are achieving their intended purpose of attracting foreign currency.

Why Is the RBI Doing This? The Rupee Problem

The answer is simple: India desperately needs dollars, and the rupee is under pressure.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have sold roughly $45 billion worth of Indian assets since 2024. In 2025 alone, foreign portfolio investors recorded net stock sales of $18.9 billion -- the biggest annual outflow since 1992. And in just the first four months of 2026, FPIs have already sold over $20 billion, surpassing the entire 2025 figure. At the same time, NRI dollar deposits in Indian banks have also fallen sharply.

When dollars flow out and do not come back in, the supply of dollars in India shrinks. This makes dollars more expensive in rupee terms -- the rupee weakens. A weaker rupee makes imports more expensive, fuels inflation, and can trigger a vicious cycle of further capital outflows.

The RBI swap facility is designed to reverse this flow. By making it extremely attractive for NRIs to deposit dollars in Indian banks -- and by removing the costs that banks normally pass on -- the RBI hopes to bring in $20 to $50 billion in fresh foreign currency deposits. SBI Research estimates the total inflow could reach $55-65 billion in FY27.

Which Banks Are Offering the Best FCNR(B) Rates Right Now?

With the rate caps removed, banks have started competing aggressively for NRI dollars. Here are the rates being offered as of late June 2026:

  • Bank of Baroda: Up to 7.40 per cent per annum (for select tenors)
  • Bandhan Bank: 7.10 per cent per annum
  • Federal Bank: Competitive rates, popular among NRIs in the Gulf region
  • Kotak Mahindra Bank: Attractive FCNR(B) rates with online NRI account opening
  • Axis Bank: Offers competitive rates with easy digital onboarding for NRIs
  • Canara Bank: 6.50 per cent per annum
  • State Bank of India (SBI): Competitive rates, typically in the 6.0-6.8 per cent range depending on currency and tenor
  • ICICI Bank: Offers competitive FCNR(B) rates, check latest on their NRI portal
  • HDFC Bank: Among the most popular choices for NRIs, rates vary by currency

Important note: These rates change frequently as banks adjust to market conditions. NRIs should check the latest rates directly with the bank or on the bank NRI portal before making a deposit. Rates also vary depending on the currency (USD, GBP, EUR, etc.) and the deposit tenure.

Which Currencies Are Allowed in FCNR(B)?

FCNR(B) deposits can be made in the following major currencies:

  • US Dollar (USD) -- Most popular, highest rates currently
  • British Pound Sterling (GBP)
  • Euro (EUR)
  • Japanese Yen (JPY)
  • Canadian Dollar (CAD)
  • Australian Dollar (AUD)
  • Singapore Dollar (SGD)
  • Swiss Franc (CHF)

The US Dollar deposits are currently offering the highest interest rates because the demand from banks is greatest for dollars. If you have earnings in other currencies, check with your bank for specific rates.

Who Is Eligible to Open an FCNR(B) Deposit?

FCNR(B) deposits are available to:

  • Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) -- Indian citizens living abroad
  • Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) -- People of Indian origin who are citizens of other countries
  • Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) -- Holders of OCI cards

You do not need an NRE or NRO account to open an FCNR(B) deposit, though most NRIs will have one. The deposit can be opened with funds transferred from your overseas bank account directly into the FCNR(B) account. Both NRE and NRO account holders are eligible -- the FCNR(B) deposit is a separate product, not a type of bank account.

NRE account holders: Can open FCNR(B) deposits by transferring funds from their NRE account. This is a popular strategy -- earn high rates on your existing NRI savings without bringing in new money from abroad.

NRO account holders: Can also open FCNR(B) deposits, but the funds must come from foreign currency sources (not from rupee balances in the NRO account). You would need to transfer fresh foreign currency from your overseas account.

FCNR(B) vs NRE vs NRO: Which Is Best for You?

This is the most common question NRIs ask. Here is a simple comparison:

FCNR(B) Deposit: Deposit in foreign currency, earn interest in foreign currency, get back in foreign currency. Zero currency risk. Interest is tax-free in India. Best for NRIs who want to keep their money in dollars (or other foreign currency) and earn a guaranteed return.

NRE Deposit: Bring foreign currency, convert to rupees, earn interest in rupees, convert back to foreign currency when you repatriate. Currency risk exists because the rupee may weaken or strengthen during your deposit period. Interest is tax-free in India. Best for NRIs who are comfortable with rupee exposure and want to benefit if the rupee strengthens.

NRO Account: Holds your India-sourced income (rent, dividends, pension) in rupees. Not for foreign currency deposits. Interest is taxable in India at applicable rates (plus TDS). Best for managing your India income, not for parking foreign savings.

The verdict: If you want safety from currency risk and a guaranteed return in dollars, FCNR(B) is currently the clear winner -- especially with the RBI new incentives. If you believe the rupee will strengthen significantly, an NRE deposit could give you extra returns from currency appreciation, but that is a bet, not a guarantee.

Pros and Cons of FCNR(B) Deposits Under the New Rules

Pros:

  • Zero currency risk: Your deposit and interest are in foreign currency. If the rupee falls 10 per cent, your deposit is unaffected
  • Tax-free interest: FCNR(B) interest is completely exempt from Indian income tax -- no TDS, no tax filing needed for this income
  • High rates: Up to 7.1-7.4 per cent on USD deposits, which is significantly higher than what US banks offer on savings or CDs
  • Fully repatriable: Both principal and interest can be freely transferred back to your country of residence
  • Safe: Deposits are held in RBI-regulated Indian banks, with DICGC insurance up to Rs. 5 lakh per depositor per bank (in rupee terms)
  • Flexible tenors: While the best rates are for 3-5 year tenors, shorter tenors from 1 year are also available

Cons:

  • Liquidity risk: Premature withdrawal may attract penalties and lower interest rates. Your money is locked in for the chosen tenure
  • Rate is temporary: The enhanced rates and zero hedging cost are available only until September 30, 2026. After that, rates may normalise
  • Bank risk: While regulated, your deposit is only as safe as the bank. Stick to large, well-capitalised banks
  • Opportunity cost: If the dollar weakens significantly against your home currency (unlikely but possible), your real return could be lower
  • No rupee upside: If the rupee strengthens, you do not benefit -- your returns are in dollars

Is FCNR(B) Better Than Other Foreign Deposits? A Detailed Comparison

This is the question every NRI should ask before parking their hard-earned foreign currency. Let us break it down with real numbers, real risks, and real alternatives. We will compare a $10,000 investment across every major option available to NRIs, using 3 years as the standard tenure.

The baseline: FCNR(B) at 7% for 3 years (compounded annually)

You deposit $10,000. After 3 years at 7% compound interest, you get $12,250.24. All of it is in US dollars. You pay zero Indian income tax. You pay zero US tax on Indian deposit interest (it is foreign-sourced income for US tax purposes, though you may need to report it). Your principal and interest are fully repatriable -- you can wire the entire $12,250 back to your US, UAE, UK, or any other bank account, anytime after maturity. No currency was ever converted. No exchange rate risk was taken.

Total return: 22.5% over 3 years. Effective annual return: 7%. Risk level: Very low.

Alternative 1: US Bank Savings Account at 4.5% for 3 years

You deposit $10,000 in a high-yield US savings account or Certificate of Deposit. After 3 years at 4.5% compound interest, you get $11,411.66. But here is the catch: this interest is taxable. If you are in the 24% US federal tax bracket (income $95,376 to $182,100 for single filers in 2026), you pay approximately $239 in federal tax on the $411.66 interest. If you also pay 5% state tax, that is another $20. Your after-tax return is approximately $11,352.

Total return: 13.5% over 3 years (after tax). Effective annual return: 4.3%. Risk level: Ultra-low (FDIC insured up to $250,000).

FCNR(B) advantage: You earn $898 more over 3 years ($12,250 vs $11,352), and your money is not stuck in the US -- it is in an Indian bank earning a higher guaranteed rate.

Alternative 2: US Treasury Bonds (3-Year) at 4.6% for 3 years

US Treasury notes are considered the safest investment in the world. A 3-year Treasury currently yields about 4.6%. After 3 years, your $10,000 becomes $11,442. Treasury interest is exempt from state and local taxes, but you still pay federal tax. At 24% bracket, you pay about $106 in federal tax. After-tax return: approximately $11,336.

Total return: 13.4% over 3 years (after tax). Effective annual return: 4.3%. Risk level: Ultra-low (US government backed).

FCNR(B) advantage: You earn $914 more over 3 years. Plus, FCNR(B) interest is completely tax-free in India, and for many NRIs in countries like UAE, Qatar, or Singapore with zero personal income tax, the FCNR(B) return is entirely tax-free globally.

Alternative 3: NRE Rupee Deposit at 6.5% for 3 years

This is where it gets interesting -- and risky. You deposit $10,000, which gets converted to rupees at the current exchange rate (say Rs. 83 per dollar = Rs. 8,30,000). At 6.5% compound interest for 3 years, this grows to approximately Rs. 10,03,000. Now you convert back to dollars. But at what rate?

Scenario A -- Rupee weakens to Rs. 90 per dollar (likely given current trends): You get $11,144. That is a total return of 11.4% over 3 years. Worse than FCNR(B).

Scenario B -- Rupee stays at Rs. 83 per dollar: You get $12,084. Total return: 20.8%. Close to FCNR(B) but not quite.

Scenario C -- Rupee strengthens to Rs. 78 per dollar (possible if FCNR inflows work): You get $12,859. Total return: 28.6%. This beats FCNR(B) significantly.

Total return: 11.4% to 28.6% depending on currency movement. Risk level: High (currency risk).

FCNR(B) advantage: Guaranteed 22.5% return with zero risk. NRE could give you more if the rupee strengthens, but it could also give you less. It is a bet, not a guarantee. For NRIs who cannot afford to lose money on currency swings, FCNR(B) is the safer choice.

Alternative 4: Indian Equity Mutual Funds (NRI Investment) for 3 years

Indian equity markets have delivered strong long-term returns. Over the past 10 years, the Nifty 50 has returned approximately 12% per annum. But over any 3-year period, the results can vary wildly. In 2020-2023, Nifty returned over 60%. In 2022-2025, it returned closer to 30%. But there have also been 3-year periods with negative returns.

If you invest $10,000 in an Indian equity fund and get 12% annual returns, you get $14,049 after 3 years. But if the market drops 20% in year one, you need a 44% return in the remaining two years just to break even. Equity investing requires a 5-7 year minimum horizon and a strong stomach for volatility.

Total return: Highly variable, -20% to +50% over 3 years. Risk level: Very high.

FCNR(B) advantage: FCNR(B) is a fixed deposit -- your return is guaranteed. Equity is not comparable unless you have a long time horizon and high risk tolerance.

Alternative 5: Foreign Currency Bonds (Emerging Market Debt Funds)

Global bond funds investing in emerging market debt currently yield around 5.5-6.5%. These funds hold government and corporate bonds from countries like India, Brazil, Indonesia, and Mexico. They offer diversification but come with currency risk, credit risk, and interest rate risk. A fund yielding 6% might return 8% in a good year or lose 5% in a bad year.

Total return: -5% to +10% over 3 years. Risk level: Moderate to high.

FCNR(B) advantage: Higher guaranteed return (7%) with lower risk (RBI-regulated bank deposit).

Alternative 6: Gold (Physical or Gold ETFs)

Gold has been a traditional favourite for Indian investors. Over the past year, gold has surged over 25%. But gold generates no income -- no interest, no dividends. Your entire return depends on price appreciation. Gold can also be volatile: it lost nearly 40% of its value between 2013 and 2015.

If you buy $10,000 worth of gold today, in 3 years it could be worth $15,000 (if the rally continues) or $8,000 (if there is a correction). There is no guarantee.

Total return: -20% to +50% over 3 years. Risk level: High.

FCNR(B) advantage: Guaranteed return with no price volatility. Gold is a hedge, not an income generator.

Alternative 7: Fixed Deposits in Your Country of Residence

If you live in the UAE, your local bank might offer 4-5% on dirham deposits. In the UK, GBP fixed deposits yield around 4-4.5%. In Canada, CAD deposits yield around 3.5-4%. In Australia, AUD deposits yield around 4-4.5%. All of these are lower than the 6.5-7.4% offered on FCNR(B) dollar deposits.

Total return: 10-15% over 3 years (varies by country). Risk level: Low.

FCNR(B) advantage: 22.5% return is significantly higher than what most local banks offer. The only consideration is whether you trust Indian banks with your money -- and for large, well-capitalised banks like SBI, ICICI, HDFC, and BoB, the risk is minimal.

The Verdict: When Is FCNR(B) the Best Choice?

After comparing every major alternative, here is when FCNR(B) wins:

  • If you want a guaranteed return in foreign currency: No other option offers 7% guaranteed in dollars with zero currency risk
  • If you want tax-free income: FCNR(B) interest is exempt from Indian tax, and for NRIs in zero-tax countries (UAE, Qatar, Singapore), it is tax-free globally
  • If you want full repatriability: Unlike some other Indian investments, every rupee (or dollar) can be freely sent back to your country of residence
  • If you want safety: RBI-regulated banks with DICGC insurance provide a level of protection that matches most developed-country bank guarantees
  • If you have a 3-5 year horizon: FCNR(B) is designed for medium-term parking of funds, not short-term trading

Here is when FCNR(B) is NOT the best choice:

  • If you need liquidity: Your money is locked in for the chosen tenure. Premature withdrawal penalties can be steep
  • If you are bullish on the rupee: If you believe the rupee will strengthen significantly, an NRE deposit could give you extra returns from currency appreciation
  • If you want equity-like returns: If you are willing to take risk for potentially higher returns, Indian equity mutual funds or direct stocks could outperform over 5-7 years
  • If you need regular income: FCNR(B) interest is typically paid at maturity (cumulative). If you need monthly or quarterly income, other options may be better

Our overall assessment: For NRIs who want a safe, guaranteed, tax-free return in foreign currency with full repatriability, the current FCNR(B) offering is arguably the best deal available anywhere in the world right now. The combination of 6.5-7.4% rates, zero currency risk, zero Indian tax, and RBI-backed safety is genuinely hard to beat. But it is a limited-time window -- the enhanced terms with zero hedging cost are available only until September 30, 2026. After that, rates may normalise closer to 4-5%, which would make the proposition less compelling compared to US Treasuries or local bank deposits.

The smart strategy: Even if you are not 100% sure about FCNR(B), consider parking a portion of your foreign currency savings -- say 20-30% -- in an FCNR(B) deposit now to lock in the high rates. Keep the rest in more liquid options like US Treasuries or your local bank. This way, you get the best of both worlds: guaranteed high returns on some money, and flexibility with the rest.

How to Open an FCNR(B) Deposit

Opening an FCNR(B) deposit is straightforward:

  • Step 1: Choose a bank. Compare rates -- Bank of Baroda, Bandhan Bank, Federal Bank, Kotak Mahindra, Axis Bank, SBI, ICICI, and HDFC are all offering competitive rates
  • Step 2: Visit the bank NRI portal or contact their NRI desk. Most banks allow you to open FCNR(B) deposits online
  • Step 3: Transfer funds from your overseas bank account to the bank FCNR(B) account via wire transfer (SWIFT)
  • Step 4: Choose your currency, tenure (1-5 years), and interest payout option (cumulative or periodic)
  • Step 5: Confirm the deposit and keep the receipt for your records

You will need your passport, visa/PIO/OCI card, and proof of NRI status. The entire process can often be completed online without visiting India.

Conclusion: Should You Act on This?

The RBI has created a rare window of opportunity for NRIs. FCNR(B) deposits are offering 6.5 to 7.4 per cent on US Dollar deposits with zero currency risk, zero Indian tax, and full repatriability. These rates are significantly higher than what you would earn in a US savings account or CD, and the tax-free status makes the effective return even more attractive.

The catch: this window is open only until September 30, 2026. After that, the interest rate caps may return, and the zero hedging cost benefit may end. If you have foreign currency savings sitting in low-yielding overseas accounts, now is the time to seriously consider moving at least a portion into FCNR(B) deposits.

That said, do not put all your eggs in one basket. Diversify across currencies, tenors, and banks. And always consult a qualified financial advisor before making significant investment decisions -- especially ones involving cross-border taxation and currency considerations.

The bottom line: for NRIs looking for a safe, high-yielding, tax-free home for their foreign currency savings, FCNR(B) deposits under the new RBI rules are worth a very serious look. The clock is ticking.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment or financial advice. FCNR(B) deposit rates, RBI rules, and tax laws are subject to change. Interest rates mentioned are based on publicly available information as of June 2026 and may vary by bank and tenure. NRIs should consult their financial advisors and tax professionals in both India and their country of residence before making investment decisions. Repatriation rules may vary by country. VilfinTV News encourages all readers to independently verify rates and rules with their bank before acting on this information.

heading: Malabar Chicken Dum Biriyani: The Complete Guide From Zero to Biriyani Hero
story:
Malabar Chicken Dum Biriyani: The Complete Guide From Zero to Biriyani Hero (With Exact Measurements, Timing, and Zero Room for Excuses)

Kitchen, June 21, 2026 -- Let us be honest. Making a proper Malabar Chicken Dum Biriyani is not cooking. It is a military operation. It is a love letter written in rice and spices. It is the reason your kitchen will smell like heaven for the next 4 hours and your neighbours will suddenly become very friendly. This is not a recipe. This is a mission. And we are going to complete it together, step by step, with exact measurements, exact timing, and absolutely zero room for the classic "I did not have that ingredient" excuse. Every spice has an alternative. Every step has a time limit. Every mistake has a rescue plan. Let us begin.

What Makes Malabar Biriyani Different (And Why It Is Worth the Effort)

Before we start chopping, let us understand what we are making. Malabar Biriyani comes from the Malabar region of Kerala -- Kozhikode, Kannur, Malappuram. It is NOT the same as Hyderabadi Biriyani. It is NOT the same as Thalassery Biriyani (though they are cousins). Malabar Biriyani uses Kaima/Jeerakasala rice (short-grain, aromatic, sticky), a gravy that is rich but not overly spicy, fried onions that are caramelized to the edge of burning, and a dum process that steams the rice and chicken together in a sealed pot until they become one entity.

The rice is not boiled separately and layered. The rice is cooked IN the gravy. The chicken is not just placed on top. The chicken is marinated, fried, and then simmered in a masala that has been built from scratch. And the dum -- the slow steam in a sealed pot -- is where the magic happens. This is what separates a good biriyani from a "I made biriyani and my family pretended to like it" biriyani.

Serves: 6 to 8 people | Total Time: 3.5 to 4 hours | Difficulty: Medium-Hard (but we will make it Easy-Medium)

Shopping List: Everything You Need (With Alternatives for Every Single Item)

Here is the complete list. Read it twice. Check your kitchen. Order what you need. No excuses later.

For the Chicken Marinade (Do this first -- it needs 1 to 2 hours):

  • Chicken (bone-in, skin-on): 1.5 kg (about 3.3 lbs), cut into 2-inch pieces -- use leg and thigh pieces for best results
  • Ginger-garlic paste: 2 tablespoons (or 1 inch ginger + 6 cloves garlic, ground together)
  • Red Kashmiri chilli powder: 1.5 tablespoons (for colour and mild heat) -- Alternative: 1 tablespoon regular chilli powder + 1 teaspoon paprika
  • Turmeric powder: 1 teaspoon
  • Biryani masala powder: 2 tablespoons (store-bought is fine) -- Alternative: Make your own -- see below
  • Curds (yogurt, whisked smooth): 1 cup (240 ml)
  • Lemon juice: 2 tablespoons
  • Salt: 1.5 teaspoons (adjust later)
  • Fresh mint leaves: 1 handful (about 20 leaves), chopped
  • Fresh coriander leaves: 1 handful, chopped

Homemade Biriyani Masala (If you do not have store-bought):

  • Black peppercorns: 1 teaspoon
  • Cloves: 4
  • Green cardamom: 4
  • Black cardamom: 1
  • Cinnamon stick: 1 inch
  • Bay leaf: 1
  • Star anise: 1 -- Alternative: Skip it, add 1 extra clove
  • Mace: 1 small piece -- Alternative: Skip or use a pinch of nutmeg
  • Shah jeera (caraway seeds): 1 teaspoon -- Alternative: Regular cumin seeds

Dry roast all for 2 minutes on low heat, then grind to a fine powder. Makes about 2.5 tablespoons.

For the Biriyani Gravy (The Soul of the Dish):

  • Onions: 4 large (about 500g), thinly sliced -- this is NOT the time to be lazy. Slice them thin and even.
  • Tomatoes: 3 medium, pureed (or finely chopped)
  • Green chillies: 4 to 6, slit lengthwise -- Alternative: 2 green chillies + 1 teaspoon crushed black pepper
  • Ginger-garlic paste: 1 tablespoon
  • Red chilli powder: 1 teaspoon (Kashmiri for colour)
  • Coriander powder: 1 tablespoon
  • Garam masala: 1 teaspoon
  • Curds (yogurt): 1/2 cup (120 ml), whisked
  • Fresh cream: 2 tablespoons -- Alternative: 2 tablespoons coconut milk (very Malabar!)
  • Ghee: 3 tablespoons -- Alternative: 2 tablespoons ghee + 1 tablespoon coconut oil
  • Vegetable oil: 3 tablespoons
  • Salt: to taste
  • Fresh mint: 1 handful
  • Fresh coriander: 1 handful

For the Rice (The Foundation):

  • Kaima/Jeerakasala rice: 500g (about 2.5 cups) -- Alternative: Basmati rice (yes, it works, but it is not authentic Malabar. We will forgive you.)
  • Water for soaking: enough to cover rice by 2 inches
  • Water for cooking: 750 ml (3 cups) -- ratio is 1:1.5 for Kaima rice
  • Ghee: 1 tablespoon
  • Bay leaf: 1
  • Cloves: 3
  • Cardamom: 2
  • Cinnamon: 1 small piece
  • Salt: 1 teaspoon
  • Lemon juice: 1 tablespoon

For the Garnish (The Bling):

  • Onions: 2 medium, sliced thin and fried until deep golden-brown (birista) -- Alternative: Store-bought fried onions (we will not tell anyone)
  • Cashew nuts: 2 tablespoons, fried in ghee until golden -- Alternative: Almonds or skip
  • Raisins: 1 tablespoon, soaked in warm water -- Alternative: Dried cranberries or skip
  • Saffron: 1 small pinch (about 15 strands), soaked in 2 tablespoons warm milk -- Alternative: 1/2 teaspoon turmeric in warm milk (for colour only, not flavour)
  • Rose water: 1 teaspoon -- Alternative: Kewra water or skip
  • Ghee: 2 tablespoons (for the final dum)

Step 1: Marinate the Chicken (Time: 5 minutes active + 1 to 2 hours waiting)

Take your chicken pieces. Wash them. Pat them dry with a clean cloth (wet chicken = steam instead of fry = sad biriyani). In a large bowl, add the chicken, ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chilli powder, turmeric, biryani masala, curds, lemon juice, salt, mint, and coriander. Mix well with your hands. Yes, your hands. This is not a spoon job. Get in there. Make sure every piece is coated. Cover the bowl with cling film and put it in the refrigerator for minimum 1 hour, maximum 2 hours. Do not skip this step. Do not marinate for 10 minutes and think it counts. The marinade needs time to penetrate the meat. Go watch a movie. Come back.

Timing note: Start marinating at Time = 0:00. You have until Time = 1:00 to 2:00 before you need the chicken again. Use this time for the next steps.

Step 2: Prepare the Rice (Time: 30 minutes soaking + 15 minutes cooking)

Take 500g Kaima rice. Wash it in 3 changes of water until the water runs mostly clear (not perfectly clear -- Kaima rice releases some starch, that is normal). Soak the rice in fresh water for exactly 30 minutes. Set a timer. Not 25 minutes. Not 35 minutes. 30 minutes.

After 30 minutes, drain the rice completely. In a large pot, bring 750 ml water to a rolling boil. Add the whole spices (bay leaf, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon), ghee, salt, and lemon juice. Add the drained rice. Stir once gently. Cook on medium heat for exactly 8 to 10 minutes until the rice is 70 per cent cooked. How do you know? Take a grain and press it. It should break but still have a slight hardness in the centre. It should NOT be soft and mushy. If it is soft, you have overcooked it and your biriyani will be a disaster. Drain the rice immediately. Spread it on a large plate to stop the cooking. Remove the whole spices (or leave them -- they will add flavour during dum).

Critical timing: The rice should be ready about 15 minutes before you are ready to layer. If it sits too long, it will dry out. If it is too hot when you layer, it will overcook in the dum. Aim for warm, not hot.

Step 3: Fry the Onions (Time: 20 to 25 minutes -- Do Not Rush This)

This is where most people fail. They fry onions for 5 minutes and call it done. No. Proper birista (fried onions) takes 20 to 25 minutes of patient stirring on medium heat. Thinly sliced onions, plenty of oil (yes, plenty -- you will drain it later). The onions will first soften, then turn golden, then turn a deep, caramelized brown. They will reduce to about 1/3 of their original volume. The oil will separate. This is when they are done.

Drain the fried onions on a paper towel. Reserve the oil -- you will use it for the gravy. You need about 1 cup of fried onions for the gravy and another 1/2 cup for the garnish. Yes, that is why we use 6 onions total.

Pro tip: If you are short on time, you can fry onions while the chicken marinates and the rice soaks. Multitasking is the biriyani way.

Step 4: Cook the Chicken (Time: 25 to 30 minutes)

Take the marinated chicken out of the fridge. Heat 3 tablespoons oil + 3 tablespoons ghee in a large, heavy-bottomed kadai or Dutch oven (this will be your biriyani pot). When the oil is hot, add the marinated chicken pieces. Do not crowd the pot. Fry in batches if needed. Fry on medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes per side until the chicken is seared and has a nice brown crust. The marinade will caramelize. This is good. Remove the chicken and set aside.

In the same oil, add the sliced onions (the 4 large ones for the gravy). Fry for 10 to 12 minutes until golden brown. Add the ginger-garlic paste and green chillies. Fry for 2 minutes. Add the tomato puree. Cook for 5 to 7 minutes until the tomatoes break down completely and the oil separates from the masala. Add the red chilli powder, coriander powder, and garam masala. Stir for 1 minute.

Now add the fried onions (about 1 cup, crushed by hand). Mix well. Add the whisked curds. Stir continuously for 2 to 3 minutes until the gravy thickens. Add the cream (or coconut milk). Mix. Add the fried chicken pieces. Coat them in the gravy. Add 1/2 cup water (just enough to create a thick gravy -- not a soup). Cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes until the chicken is 80 per cent cooked and the gravy is thick and rich.

Test: The gravy should coat the back of a spoon. If it is too thin, cook uncovered for 5 more minutes. If it is too thick, add 2 tablespoons water. Taste the gravy. It should be well-spiced, slightly tangy from the curds, and rich. Adjust salt.

Remove from heat. The chicken should be sitting in a thick, aromatic gravy. This is your biriyani base.

Step 5: Layer the Biriyani (Time: 10 minutes -- The Most Important 10 Minutes)

Take the same pot with the chicken gravy (or transfer to a heavy-bottomed pot if your kadai is not oven-safe). Spread the chicken and gravy evenly at the bottom. Spread the 70 per cent cooked rice evenly over the chicken. Do not mix. The rice sits ON TOP of the chicken.

Now the garnish: Sprinkle the remaining fried onions, fried cashews, soaked raisins, and saffron milk over the rice. Drizzle 2 tablespoons ghee. Sprinkle the rose water. Add a final handful of fresh mint and coriander.

Photo close-up: The top layer showing golden fried onions, saffron streaks, green mint leaves, and white rice grains.

Step 6: The Dum (Time: 25 to 30 minutes -- The Grand Finale)

This is it. The moment of truth. The dum is what transforms layered rice and chicken into biriyani.

Cover the pot with a tight-fitting lid. If your lid is not tight enough, seal the edges with aluminium foil, then place the lid on top. The goal is to trap ALL the steam inside.

Place the pot on the lowest possible flame. Not medium. Not medium-low. The absolute lowest. If you have a flame diffuser (tawa), place it under the pot. Cook for 25 minutes. Do not open the lid. Do not peek. Do not "just check." The steam is doing its job. Trust the process.

After 25 minutes, turn off the heat. Let the pot sit, covered, for 10 more minutes. This resting period allows the flavours to settle and the rice to finish cooking in the residual steam.

Step 7: The Reveal (Time: 2 minutes -- The Best 2 Minutes of Your Life)

Remove the lid. The smell will hit you like a wave. Gently mix the rice and chicken from the bottom, being careful not to break the rice grains. Transfer to a serving dish. Garnish with remaining fried onions, fresh mint, and a drizzle of ghee.

Photo: The finished biriyani in a large serving dish, with a spoon showing the individual rice grains and a piece of chicken. Raita and pickle visible on the side.

Serve with: Cucumber raita (grated cucumber + curds + roasted cumin + salt), Malabar pickle (mango or lemon), and papad (fried, not roasted -- we are not animals).

The Complete Timing Chart (Print This and Stick It on Your Fridge)

  • 0:00 to 0:05: Marinate chicken, put in fridge
  • 0:05 to 0:35: Soak rice (30 min)
  • 0:05 to 0:30: Fry all onions (25 min) -- do this while rice soaks
  • 0:30 to 0:35: Fry cashews and raisins (5 min)
  • 0:35 to 0:45: Soak saffron in warm milk (10 min)
  • 0:35 to 0:50: Cook rice (10 min boil + 5 min drain and spread)
  • 0:50 to 1:20: Cook chicken and gravy (30 min)
  • 1:20 to 1:30: Layer biriyani (10 min)
  • 1:30 to 1:55: Dum on low flame (25 min)
  • 1:55 to 2:05: Rest with lid on (10 min)
  • 2:05: OPEN THE LID AND BECOME A LEGEND

Total active time: about 1.5 hours | Total elapsed time: about 2 hours | Resting/marinating time: 1 to 2 hours (mostly hands-off)

Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Mistake 1: Overcooking the rice before dum. If your rice is 100 per cent cooked before it goes into the dum, it will turn to mush. 70 per cent cooked means the grain breaks when pressed but still has a tiny hard centre. The dum finishes the cooking.

Mistake 2: Too much water in the gravy. The gravy should be thick, not soupy. Excess water will make the rice soggy. If your gravy is too thin, cook it uncovered for 5 to 10 minutes before layering.

Mistake 3: High flame during dum. This is the #1 biriyani killer. The bottom will burn while the top stays raw. Lowest flame. Always.

Mistake 4: Opening the lid during dum. Every time you open the lid, you release steam and drop the temperature. The dum needs constant, gentle heat. Leave it alone.

Mistake 5: Using the wrong rice. Kaima/Jeerakasala rice is non-negotiable for authentic Malabar biriyani. It is short-grain, aromatic, and absorbs the gravy beautifully. Basmati will give you a different (not bad, just different) result.

Mistake 6: Skipping the marination. 1 hour minimum. The marinade tenderizes the chicken and infuses it with flavour. 10 minutes is not marination. It is a brief introduction.

The Comedy Section: What Will Go Wrong and How to Laugh About It

Let us be real. Even with perfect instructions, things will go wrong. Here is what to expect:

Your first attempt will not be Instagram-perfect. The rice might be slightly overcooked. The chicken might be slightly under-gravied. The onions might be slightly burnt. It will still taste amazing. Biriyani is forgiving. It wants you to succeed.

Your kitchen will look like a crime scene. Onion skins on the floor. Turmeric stains on your counter. Ghee splatters on your ceiling (okay, maybe not the ceiling). This is normal. This is the biriyani tax. Clean up later. Eat first.

Your family will gather in the kitchen. They will ask "Is it ready yet?" every 5 minutes. They will try to peek under the lid. They will "taste test" the gravy (which is actually a good idea -- taste and adjust salt before layering). Shoo them away during the dum. They can wait.

You will eat too much. This is guaranteed. Biriyani has a gravitational pull. You will say "just one more piece" four times. Your stomach will file a complaint. You will ignore it. This is the biriyani experience.

Final Words: The Biriyani Philosophy

Making Malabar Chicken Dum Biriyani is not about perfection. It is about patience, love, and the willingness to spend 2 hours in a kitchen for 15 minutes of eating bliss. It is about the smell that fills your home. It is about the moment you lift the lid and the steam carries the aroma of saffron, ghee, fried onions, and slow-cooked chicken to every corner of your house.

It is about serving it to people you love and watching their eyes light up. It is about the silence that falls over the table for the first 5 minutes because everyone is too busy eating to talk.

That is what biriyani is. That is why we make it. That is why it is worth every minute, every ingredient, and every dirty dish.

Now go make biriyani. And when you do, remember: low flame, tight lid, and trust the dum.

Disclaimer: This recipe is provided for informational and entertainment purposes. Cooking times may vary based on your stove, pot size, and altitude. The author is not responsible for any biriyani-related happiness, family arguments over the last piece, or the inability to eat normal food after tasting proper Malabar Biriyani. All spice alternatives are suggestions -- adjust to your taste and availability. If you burn the onions, start over. There is no rescue plan for burnt onions. We are serious about that.

മലബാർ ചിക്കൻ ഡം ബിരിയാണി: ആംഗ്യത്തിൽ നിന്ന് ബിരിയാണി നായകനിലേക്ക്

അടുക്കള, ജൂൺ 21, 2026 -- നമ്മൾ ഒരു ശരിയായ മലബാർ ചിക്കൻ ഡം ബിരിയാണി ഉണ്ടാക്കാൻ പോകുന്നു. ഇത് പാചകമല്ല -- ഇത് ഒരു സൈനിക നടപടിക്രമമാണ്. അരിയിലും മസാലകളിലും എഴുതിയ ഒരു പ്രണയക്ത. നിങ്ങളുടെ അടുക്കള അടുപ്പിക്കാൻ ഇടയാകും. പക്ഷേ ഫലം കാണാൻ ക്ഷമയുണ്ടാകണം. ഇത് ഒരു പാചകക്കുറിപ്പല്ല -- ഇത് ഒരു ദൗത്യം. ഘട്ടം ഘട്ടമായി, കൃത്യമായ അളവുകളോടെ, കൃത്യമായ സമയക്രമത്തോടെ, "എന്റെ അടുക്കളിൽ അത് ഇല്ല" എന്ന ഒഴിവും ഇല്ലാതെ. ഓരോ സുഗന്ധവ്യഞ്ജനത്തിനും ബദൾ ഉണ്ട്. ഓരോ ഘട്ടത്തിനും സമയപരിധി ഉണ്ട്. നമുക്ക് തുടങ്ങാം.

മലബാർ ബിരിയാണി എന്തുകൊണ്ട് വ്യത്യസ്തം

ആദം ചെയ്യുന്നതിന് മുമ്പ്, നമ്മൾ എന്ത് ഉണ്ടാക്കുന്നു എന്ന് മനസ്സിലാക്കാം. മലബാർ ബിരിയാണി കേരളത്തിലെ മലബാർ മേഖലയിൽ നിന്ന് വരുന്നു -- കോഴിക്കോട്, കണ്ണൂർ, മലപ്പുറം. ഇത് ഹൈദരാബാദി ബിരിയാണി അല്ല. തലശ്ശേരി ബിരിയാണി അല്ല. മലബാർ ബിരിയാണി കൈമ/ജീരകശാല അരി ഉപയോഗിക്കുന്നു -- ചെറിയ ധാന്യം, സുഗന്ധമുള്ളത്, ഗ്രവി ആഗിരണം ചെയ്യുന്നത്. അരി വേർതിരിച്ച് തിളപ്പിച്ച് പാളി ആക്കുന്നതല്ല -- അരി ഗ്രവിക്കുള്ളിൽ മസാലയോടെയാണ് പൊരിക്കുന്നത്. ചിക്കൻ മുകളിൽ വയ്ക്കുന്നതല്ല -- മാരിനേറ്റ് ചെയ്ത് വറുത്ത് മസാലയിൽ ചുട്ടെടുക്കുന്നു. ഡം -- അടയ്ക്കിയ പാത്രത്തിൽ ഈർപ്പത്തിൽ അരിയും ചിക്കനും ഒന്നാകുന്നു. ഇതാണ് നല്ല ബിരിയാണിയെ "ബിരിയാണി ഉണ്ടാക്കി, കുടുംബം ഇഷ്ടമായ നടിച്ചു" എന്നതിൽ നിന്ന് വേർതിരിക്കുന്നത്.

സേവനം: 6 മുതൽ 8 പേർ വരെ | മൊത്തം സമയം: 3.5 മുതൽ 4 മണിക്കൂർ | ബുദ്ധിമുട്ട്: ഇടത്തരം (ഞങ്ങൾ എളുപ്പമാക്കും)

വാങ്ങേണ്ട സാധനങ്ങൾ (ഓരോ ഇനത്തിനും ബദൾ സഹിതം)

ചിക്കൻ മാരിനേഷൻ (ആദ്യം ഇത് ചെയ്യണം -- 1 മുതൽ 2 മണിക്കൂർ ആവശ്യം):

  • ചിക്കൻ (എല്ലുള്ള, തൊലിയുള്ള): 1.5 കിലോഗ്രാം, 2 ഇഞ്ച് കഷണങ്ങളായി -- കാലും തുടയും ഉപയോഗിക്കാം
  • ഇഞ്ചി-വെളുത്തുള്ളി പേസ്റ്റ്: 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ (അല്ലെങ്കിൽ 1 ഇഞ്ച് ഇഞ്ചി + 6 ഗ്രാമ്പൂ, അരച്ചെടുക്കുക)
  • കാശ്മീരി ചുവന്നുള്ളി പൊടി: 1.5 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ (നിറത്തിനും നേരിയ ചൂടിനും) -- ബദൽ: 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ സാധാരണ മല്ലി പൊടി + 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ പപ്രിക
  • മഞ്ളൾ പൊടി: 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ
  • ബിരിയാണി മസാല പൊടി: 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ (കടയിൽ നിന്ന് വാങ്ങിയത് മതി) -- ബദൽ: സ്വന്തമായി ഉണ്ടാക്കുക
  • തൈര് (കുടച്ചെടുത്തത്): 1 കപ്പ് (240 ml)
  • നാരങ്ങാനീർ: 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ
  • ഉപ്പ്: 1.5 ടീസ്പൂൺ (പിന്നീട് ക്രമീകരിക്കാം)
  • പുദ്ദീന ഇല: ഒരു പിടി, അരിഞ്ഞത്
  • മല്ലി ഇല: ഒരു പിടി, അരിഞ്ഞത്

സ്വന്തം ബിരിയാണി മസാല: കുരുമുളക് 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ, ഗ്രാമ്പൂ 4, ഏലക്ക 4, കോട്ടമുളക് 1, കറുവാപ്പട്ട 1 ഇഞ്ച്, വയനാടു ഇല 1, നക്ഷത്ര തക്കോലം 1 (ബദൽ: ഒഴിവാക്കുക), ജാവിത്രി ഒരു ചെറിയ കഷണം (ബദൽ: ഒഴിവാക്കുക), ശാഹി ജീരകം 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ (ബദൽ: സാധാരണ ജീരകം). എല്ലാം 2 മിനിറ്റ് വറുത്ത് പൊടിക്കുക.

ഗ്രവി: സവാള 4 വലിയത് (500 ഗ്രാം), തക്കാളി 3, പച്ചമുളക് 4-6, ഇഞ്ചി-വെളുത്തുള്ളി പേസ്റ്റ് 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ, ചുവന്നുള്ളി പൊടി 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ, മല്ലിപ്പൊടി 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ, ഗരം മസാല 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ, തൈര് 1/2 കപ്പ്, ക്രീം 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ (ബദൽ: തേങ്ങാപ്പാൽ), നെയ്യ് 3 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ (ബദൽ: തേങ്ങയെണ്ണ), എണ്ണ 3 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ.

അരി: കൈമ/ജീരകശാല 500 ഗ്രാം (ബദൽ: ബസ്മതി), വെള്ളം 750 ml, നെയ്യ് 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ, വയനാടു ഇല 1, ഗ്രാമ്പൂ 3, ഏലക്ക 2, കറുവാപ്പട്ട 1, ഉപ്പ് 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ, നാരങ്ങാനീർ 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ.

അലങ്കാരം: സവാള 2 (വറുത്തത്), കശുവണ്ടി 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ, ഉണക്കമുന്തിരി 1 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ, കുങ്കുമപ്പുവ് ചൂടുപാലിൽ, പനിനീർ 1 ടീസ്പൂൺ, നെയ്യ് 2 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ.

ഘട്ടം 1: ചിക്കൻ മാരിനേറ്റ് (5 മിനിറ്റ് + 1-2 മണിക്കൂർ)

ചിക്കൻ കഴുകി വരണ്ട തുണിയിൽ തലപ്പിക്കുക. ഒരു വലിയ പാത്രത്തിൽ എല്ലാ മസാലകളും ചേർത്ത് കൈകൊണ്ട് ഇളക്കുക. ക്ലിംഗ് ഫിലിം വച്ച് റഫ്രിഡ്ജറേറ്ററിൽ വയ്ക്കുക. കുറഞ്ഞത് 1 മണിക്കൂർ. ഈ സമയത്ത് സവാള വറുത്തെടുക്കാം, അരി കുതിര്ക്കാം.

ഘട്ടം 2: അരി തയ്യാറാക്കുക (30 മിനിറ്റ് കുതിര്പ്പ് + 15 മിനിറ്റ്)

500 ഗ്രാം കൈമ അരി 3 തവണ കഴുകി 30 മിനിറ്റ് കുതിര്ക്കുക. ടൈമർ വയ്ക്കുക. 30 മിനിറ്റ് കൃത്യം. വെള്ളം കളയുക. 750 ml വെള്ളം തിളപ്പിച്ച് മസാലകളും നെയ്യും ഉപ്പും ചേർത്ത് അരി പൊരിക്കുക. ഇടത്തര തീയിൽ 8-10 മിനിറ്റ്. അരി 70% മാത്രം പൊരിക്കണം. ധാന്യം ഉടിക്കുമ്പോഴും നടുവിൽ ചെറിയ കഠിനത ഉണ്ടാകണം. ഉടനെ വെള്ളം കളയ്ക്കുക. പ്ലേറ്റിൽ വിതറുക.

ഘട്ടം 3: സവാള വറുത്തെടുക്കുക (20-25 മിനിറ്റ്)

ഇവിടെയാണ് മിക്കവരും തെറ്റുന്നത്. 5 മിനിറ്റ് വറുത്ത് "സവാള തയ്യാര്" എന്ന് പറയരുത്. 20-25 മിനിറ്റ് സഹിഷ്ണുതയോടെ ഇളക്കണം. നേർത്തതായി അരിഞ്ഞ സവാള, ധാരാളം എണ്ണ, ഇടത്തര തീ. സവാള മൃദുവാകും, സ്വർണ്ണ നിറമാകും, കരമെൽ തവിട്ട് ആകും. യഥാർത്ഥ അളവിന്റെ മൂന്നിലൊന്നിലേക്ക് കുറയും. എണ്ണ വേർതിരികും. പേപ്പർ ടവലിൽ എണ്ണ കളയുക. ഗ്രവിക്ക് 1 കപ്പ്, അലങ്കാരത്തിന് 1/2 കപ്പ് വേണം.

ഘട്ടം 4: ചിക്കനും ഗ്രവിയും (25-30 മിനിറ്റ്)

3 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ എണ്ണ + 3 ടേബിൾസ്പൂൺ നെയ്യ് ചൂടാക്കുക. മാരിനേറ്റ് ചെയ്ത ചിക്കൻ ബാച്ചുകളായി വറുത്തെടുക്കുക (ഓരോ വശത്തും 4-5 മിനിറ്റ്). അതേ എണ്ണയിൽ സവാള 10-12 മിനിറ്റ് വറുത്തെടുക്കുക. ഇഞ്ചി-വെളുത്തുള്ളി പേസ്റ്റും പച്ചമുളകും ചേർത്ത് 2 മിനിറ്റ് വറുത്തെടുക്കുക. തക്കാളി പേസ്റ്റ് ചേർത്ത് 5-7 മിനിറ്റ് (എണ്ണ വേർതിരികുന്നതുവരെ) വെക്കുക. ചുവന്നുള്ളി പൊടി, മല്ലിപ്പൊടി, ഗരം മസാല ചേർത്ത് 1 മിനിറ്റ് ഇളക്കുക. വറുത്ത സവാള (1 കപ്പ്, ചതച്ചത്) ചേർക്കുക. കുടച്ചെടുത്ത തൈര് ചേർത്ത് 2-3 മിനിറ്റ് ഇളക്കുക. ക്രീം ചേർക്കുക. വറുത്ത ചിക്കൻ ചേർത്ത് ഗ്രവിയിൽ മുക്കിമറിക്കുക. 1/2 കപ്പ് വെള്ളം ചേർത്ത് മൂടി കുറഞ്ഞ തീയിൽ 15 മിനിറ്റ് വെക്കുക. ചിക്കൻ 80%, ഗ്രവി കട്ടിയും സമൃദ്ധവും ആയിരിക്കണം. രുചി പരിശോധിച്ച് ഉപ്പ് ക്രമീകരിക്കുക.

ഘട്ടം 5: പാളി ആക്കുക (10 മിനിറ്റ്)

ചിക്കനും ഗ്രവിയും പാത്രത്തിന്റെ അടിയിൽ ഒരുപോലെ ഇടുക. 70% പൊരിച്ച അരി മുകളിൽ പടരുത്തുക. ഇളക്കരുത്. ബാക്കിയുള്ള വറുത്ത സവാള, കശുവണ്ടി, ഉണക്കമുന്തിരി, കുങ്കുമപ്പുവ് പാൽ, നെയ്യ് മുകളിൽ ചിതറിക്കുക. പനിനീർ തളിക്കുക. പുദ്ദീനയും മല്ലിയും ചേർക്കുക.

ഘട്ടം 6: ഡം (25-30 മിനിറ്റ്)

ഇതാണ് സത്യത്തിന്റെ നിമിഷം. പാളി ആക്കിയ അരിയെയും ചിക്കനെയും ബിരിയാണിയാക്കി മാറ്റുന്നത് ഡം ആണ്. പാത്രം കർശനമായ മൂടികൊണ്ട് മൂടുക. മൂടി ഇല്ലെങ്കിൽ അലുമിനിയം ഫോയിൽ വച്ച് അടയ്ക്കുക. എല്ലാ ആവിയും അകത്ത് കെട്ടിയിരിക്കണം. ഏറ്റവും കുറഞ്ഞ തീ. 25 മിനിറ്റ്. മൂടി ഉയർത്തരുത്. ആവിയെ വിശ്വസിക്കുക. 25 മിനിറ്റിന് ശേഷം തീ ഓഫ്. 10 മിനിറ്റ് കൂടി ഇരിക്കട്ടെ.

ഘട്ടം 7: വെളിപ്പെടുത്തൽ

മൂടി ഉയർത്തുക. മണം നിങ്ങളെ ആക്രമിക്കും. താഴെ നിന്ന് മൃദുവായി ഇളക്കുക. സേവന പാത്രത്തിൽ മാറ്റുക. വറുത്ത സവാള, പുദ്ദീന, നെയ്യ് ചേർക്കുക. കുക്കുമ്പർ റൈത, മലബാർ അച്ചാർ, പപ്പടം സഹിതം സേവിക്കുക.

സമയക്രമ ചാർട്ട്

  • 0:00-0:05: മാരിനേറ്റ് ചെയ്ത് റഫ്രിഡ്ജറേറ്ററിൽ വയ്ക്കുക
  • 0:05-0:35: അരി കുതിര്ക്കുക (30 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 0:05-0:30: സവാള വറുത്തെടുക്കുക (25 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 0:35-0:50: അരി പൊരിക്കുക (10+5 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 0:50-1:20: ചിക്കൻ + ഗ്രവി (30 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 1:20-1:30: പാളി ആക്കുക (10 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 1:30-1:55: ഡം കുറഞ്ഞ തീയിൽ (25 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 1:55-2:05: മൂടിയുള്ള പാത്രം ഇരിക്കട്ടെ (10 മിനിറ്റ്)
  • 2:05: മൂടി ഉയർത്തി നായകനാകുക

സാധാരണ തെറ്റുകൾ

1. അരി അമിതം പൊരിക്കുക: 70% മാത്രം പൊരിക്കണം. ബാക്കി ഡം പൂർത്തിയാക്കും.
2. ഗ്രവിയിൽ വെള്ളം കൂടുതൽ: കട്ടിയുള്ള ഗ്രവി വേണം.
3. ഡത്തിൽ ഉയർന്ന തീ: താഴെ കരിയും. ഏറ്റവും കുറഞ്ഞ തീ. എപ്പോഴും.
4. ഡത്തിനിടയിൽ മൂടി ഉയർത്തുക: ആവി പോകും. ഒറ്റിക്കുക.
5. തെറ്റായ അരി: കൈമ/ജീരകശാല നിർണായകം.
6. മാരിനേഷൻ ഒഴിവാക്കുക: കുറഞ്ഞത് 1 മണിക്കൂർ.

കോമഡി ഭാഗം: എന്തെല്ലാം സംഭവിക്കും

നേരും തെളിയും പറയാം. തികച്ചും നിർദ്ദേശങ്ങളുണ്ടെങ്കിലും, സംഭവിക്കും:

നിങ്ങളുടെ ആദ്യ ശ്രമം സോഷ്യൽ മീഡിയയിൽ പോസ്റ്റ് ചെയ്യാനുള്ള രീതിയിൽ ആകില്ല. അരി അൽപ്പം അധികം പൊരിച്ചേക്കാം. സവാള അൽപ്പം കരിഞ്ഞേക്കാം. എന്നാലും രുചി നന്നായിരിക്കും -- ബിരിയാണി ക്ഷമിക്കുന്നു.

നിങ്ങളുടെ അടുക്കള ഒരു കുറ്റകൃത്യ സ്ഥലം പോലെ ആകും. സവാളയുടെ തൊലി തറയിൽ. മഞ്ളൾ കൗണ്ടറിൽ തേച്ചുകെട്ടി. പിന്നീട് വൃത്തിയാക്കാം. ആദ്യം ഭക്ഷിക്കാം.

നിങ്ങളുടെ കുടുംബം അടുക്കളിൽ നിറയും. "ഇനിയും എത്ര സമയം?" എന്ന് ഓരോ 5 മിനിറ്റിലും ചോദിക്കും. കൊച്ചു കുട്ടികൾ മൂടി കാണാൻ ശ്രമിക്കും. ഡത്തിന് സമീപപ്പെടരുത് -- ഇവർക്ക് കാത്തിരിക്കാൻ കഴിയില്ല.

നിങ്ങൾ അമിതം ഭക്ഷിക്കും. ഇത് ഉറപ്പാണ്. ബിരിയാണിക്ക് ഒരു ഗുരുത്വാകർഷണം ഉണ്ട്. "ഇനിയും ഒരു കഷണം" എന്ന് 4 തവണ പറയും. വയറ് പരാതി പറയും. അവഗണിക്കുക. ഇതാണ് ബിരിയാണി അനുഭവം.

ബിരിയാണി തത്വശാസ്ത്രം

മലബാർ ചിക്കൻ ഡം ബിരിയാണി ഉണ്ടാക്കുക എന്നത് പൂർത്തിയായ ആരാധനയാണ്. ക്ഷമ, സ്നേഹം, അടുക്കളിൽ 2 മണിക്കൂർ നിന്നിരിക്കാൻ തയ്യാറാകൽ. വീട് നിറയുന്ന മണ്. മൂടി ഉയർത്തുമ്പോൾ കണ്ണുകൾ കളിയാക്കുന്ന അരോമ.

സ്നേഹം ഉള്ള ആളുകൾക്ക് സേവിക്കുക. ആദ്യ 5 മിനിറ്റ് മൗനം -- എല്ലാവരും ഭക്ഷിക്കുന്നതിനായി. അതാണ് ബിരിയാണി.

ഇപ്പോൾ പോയി ബിരിയാണി ഉണ്ടാക്കുക. കുറഞ്ഞ തി, കർശനമായ മൂടി, ഡത്തിനെ വിശ്വസിക്കുക.

നിരാകരണം: ഈ പാചകക്കുറിപ്പ് വിവരണാത്മകവും വിനോദാത്മകവുമായ ആവശ്യങ്ങൾക്ക് മാത്രം. പാചക സമയം നിങ്ങളുടെ അടുപ്പ്, പാത്രം, ഉയരം എന്നിവയെ ആശ്രയിച്ച് മാറാം. കുറിച്ച ബിരിയാണി സന്തോഷം, കുടുംബ തർക്കങ്ങൾ (അവസാന കഷണത്തിനായി), അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ശരിയായ മലബാർ ബിരിയാണി കഴിച്ച ശേഷം സാധാരണ ഭക്ഷണം കഴിക്കാൻ കഴിയാതിരിക്കൽ എന്നിവയ്ക്ക് ലേഖകൻ ഉത്തരവാദിയല്ല. എല്ലാ മസാല ബദലുകളും നിർദ്ദേശങ്ങൾ മാത്രം -- നിങ്ങളുടെ രുചിക്ക് അനുസരിച്ച് ക്രമീകരിക്കുക. സവാള കരിഞ്ഞാൽ പുതിയത് തുടങ്ങുക. കരിഞ്ഞ സവാളയ്ക്ക് രക്ഷയില്ല. ഞങ്ങൾ ഇതിനെക്കുറിച്ച് ഗുരുതരമാണ്.

heading: India's Airport Revolution: The Trillion-Rupee Bet on Becoming the World's Next Great Aviation Hub
story:
The vast, column-free expanse of Terminal 3 at Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi hums with a controlled chaos that would overwhelm the uninitiated. At 4:30 in the morning, long before the sun crests the smog-laden horizon of the National Capital Region, thousands of passengers stream through its gleaming corridors — business travellers in crisp suits bound for London and Dubai, families laden with luggage heading to Toronto and Singapore, and a growing cohort of transit passengers from Europe who are discovering that Delhi offers a faster, cheaper, and increasingly more pleasant connection to Southeast Asia than the long-established hubs of the Gulf. The terminal, which opened in 2010 and was then the eighth-largest in the world, now feels almost quaint compared to what is being planned around it. Above them, a digital display board flickers with departures to 150 international destinations, a number that has tripled in the last decade alone. This is not merely an airport; it is the beating heart of a nation's audacious ambition to become the undisputed aviation superpower of the twenty-first century.

India's airport revolution is not a single story but a constellation of them, unfolding simultaneously across a subcontinent of 1.4 billion people. From the dusty construction sites of Jewar in Uttar Pradesh, where the foundations of what will become one of the world's largest airports are being laid, to the coastal plains of Navi Mumbai, where a second gateway to India's financial capital is rising from reclaimed land, the scale of investment is staggering. The Airports Authority of India, alongside private operators like GMR Group, GVK, and the Adani Group, is overseeing capital expenditure exceeding ₹2.5 trillion (approximately $30 billion) over the current decade. This is not merely about building terminals and runways; it is about reimagining the very geography of global air travel at a moment when the centre of gravity of the aviation industry is shifting inexorably eastward.

The numbers tell a compelling story. India is already the world's third-largest domestic aviation market, having overtaken both the United Kingdom and Japan in the last five years. Passenger traffic, which stood at 187 million in 2014, surpassed 370 million in 2024 and is projected to exceed 700 million by 2030. International traffic, long the neglected stepchild of Indian aviation, is growing even faster, with double-digit percentage increases year-on-year. The International Air Transport Association has predicted that India will surpass China as the world's largest aviation market by passenger volume before 2040. But behind these headline figures lies a more nuanced and arguably more important transformation: the deliberate, state-sponsored effort to convert India's airports from mere points of origin and arrival into genuine international transit hubs that can compete with Dubai, Doha, Istanbul, and Singapore for the lucrative connecting traffic between Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

The soaring interior of Terminal 3 at Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi — a facility that has become the flagship of India's aviation ambitions, handling over 70 million passengers annually and serving as the primary gateway for international transit traffic.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The Jewel of Jewar: Building the World's Largest Airport

Some 80 kilometres southeast of central Delhi, in the agrarian hinterland of Uttar Pradesh's Gautam Buddh Nagar district, a construction site of almost incomprehensible scale is taking shape. The Noida International Airport at Jewar, named after the freedom fighter Raja Ram Jat, is not merely another airport — it is a statement of intent. When its first phase becomes operational in late 2026, it will feature two parallel runways and a terminal capable of handling 12 million passengers per annum. But that is merely the opening act. The master plan envisions, over three decades of phased development, a colossal facility with eight runways and a ultimate capacity of 120 million passengers per year, which would make it the largest airport in the world by both physical footprint and throughput, surpassing Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson and Dubai's Al Maktoum International.

The project is being developed by Zurich Airport International AG, which won the public-private partnership concession in 2019, in collaboration with the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority. The total investment is estimated at ₹29,560 crore (approximately $3.6 billion) for the first phase alone, with the full build-out expected to cost upwards of ₹1 trillion. What makes Jewar strategically significant is not merely its size but its location. Situated on the Yamuna Expressway, it will serve not only the 6 million residents of Noida and Greater Noida but also act as a relief valve for Delhi's IGIA, which has been operating beyond its designed capacity for several years. More importantly, its proximity to the Dedicated Freight Corridor and the upcoming Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor positions it as a potential cargo hub of global significance.

The design philosophy behind Jewar represents a generational leap from existing Indian airports. The terminal, conceived by the Nordic architecture firm Nordic — Office of Architecture, draws inspiration from India's traditional stepwells and courtyard houses, translating these into a modern aviation context. The roof structure, a sweeping series of interconnected vaults, is designed to maximise natural light while minimising solar gain — a critical consideration in a region where summer temperatures routinely exceed 45 degrees Celsius. Sustainability is embedded in the project's DNA: the airport aims to be carbon-neutral from its first day of operations, with extensive solar farms, rainwater harvesting systems, and zero single-use plastic policies. A 40-megawatt solar park will supply a significant portion of the airport's electricity needs, while treated wastewater will be used for irrigation and cooling.

But Jewar's ambitions extend far beyond passenger handling. The master plan includes a dedicated cargo complex spanning 1,000 acres, with the capacity to process 2.5 million tonnes of freight annually by 2030. This is a direct challenge to the established cargo hubs of Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Dubai, and it leverages India's growing role in global supply chains, particularly in pharmaceuticals, electronics, and perishable agricultural products. The airport's location at the intersection of multiple expressway and rail corridors means that goods arriving by air can be distributed across the vast northern Indian market — home to over 500 million consumers — within hours. The Uttar Pradesh government has designated a 14,000-hectare aerotropolis around the airport, with special economic zones, logistics parks, and manufacturing clusters designed to create an aviation-centric economic ecosystem.

Navi Mumbai: A Second Gateway for a Megalopolis

On the opposite side of the country, another mega-project is reshaping the aviation landscape. The Navi Mumbai International Airport, located in the Panvel area of Maharashtra's Raigad district, is designed to address a problem that has plagued India's commercial capital for decades: the chronic congestion of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport. Mumbai's existing airport, a single-runway facility hemmed in by dense urban development, handles over 50 million passengers per year on infrastructure designed for less than half that number. The result is some of the longest taxiway delays in Asia, constrained slot availability, and a ceiling on growth that has forced airlines to look elsewhere for expansion. Navi Mumbai will change that equation entirely.

The project, being developed by Navi Mumbai International Airport Limited — a joint venture between the Adani Group (which holds a 74% stake) and the City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra (CIDCO) — involves the construction of two parallel runways, each 3,700 metres long, capable of handling the world's largest aircraft simultaneously. The first phase, expected to become operational in 2027, will handle 20 million passengers annually, with the ultimate capacity reaching 90 million upon full completion. The total project cost is estimated at ₹16,700 crore ($2 billion), making it one of the largest infrastructure investments in Maharashtra's history. The airport's design, by the London-based firm Zaha Hadid Architects, features a series of interconnected terminal buildings with a distinctive wing-like roof structure that evokes the image of a bird in flight — a fitting metaphor for a city that has always looked outward to the world.

The connectivity infrastructure being built around Navi Mumbai Airport is as impressive as the airport itself. The Navi Mumbai Metro's Line 1 will connect the airport to the city's rapidly expanding suburban rail network, while the Mumbai Trans-Harbour Link — India's longest sea bridge, connecting Mumbai with Navi Mumbai — will reduce travel time between the two cities from over 90 minutes to less than 20. A dedicated airport express line on the Mumbai Metro network is also planned, along with a new coastal road that will provide a high-speed corridor to South Mumbai. The airport's integration with the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, India's largest container port, through a dedicated freight corridor creates a sea-air multimodal logistics hub that could transform Mumbai into a global supply chain node rivalling Singapore and Rotterdam.

The international terminal at Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, which has been operating beyond its designed capacity for years — a problem that the new Navi Mumbai International Airport is designed to solve.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The Southern Quadrant: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Cochin Lead the Charge

While Delhi and Mumbai dominate the headlines, some of the most transformative developments in Indian aviation are occurring in the southern states, where a combination of technology industry growth, progressive state governance, and strategic geographic positioning is creating a new generation of international hubs. Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru, the capital of Karnataka and India's technology capital, has emerged as perhaps the most dynamic airport in the country, a facility that has grown from a single-terminal, 7-million-passenger operation in 2008 to a dual-terminal complex handling over 40 million passengers in 2024. The airport's second terminal, designed by the American firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, is a 255,000-square-metre behemoth that will eventually push the airport's capacity to 65 million passengers per annum, with a further expansion to 90 million planned for the 2030s.

Bengaluru's significance as an aviation hub extends far beyond its passenger numbers. The city is home to over 400 multinational technology companies, a thriving startup ecosystem, and a large expatriate community that generates substantial business travel demand. The airport has capitalised on this by developing direct connections to every major global technology hub — San Francisco, Seattle, London, Singapore, Tokyo — and by positioning itself as the preferred gateway for the Indian diaspora in North America and Europe. The airport's cargo operations have grown in parallel, with dedicated facilities for pharmaceutical shipments, electronics, and perishable goods, leveraging Bengaluru's position as a major manufacturing and research centre. The Karnataka government's decision to develop a 5,000-acre aerospace special economic zone adjacent to the airport has attracted investments from Boeing, Airbus, and Honeywell, creating an aviation ecosystem that extends far beyond the terminal building.

Hyderabad's Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, operated by the GMR Group, has undergone a similarly dramatic transformation. Once a modest facility serving a mid-sized Indian city, it has grown into a major international hub handling over 25 million passengers annually, with a recently completed expansion adding 12 million passengers of additional capacity. The airport's cargo terminal, which handles over 180,000 tonnes annually, has become a critical node in global pharmaceutical supply chains, with dedicated cold-chain facilities capable of maintaining temperatures as low as minus 80 degrees Celsius — essential for the transport of mRNA vaccines and other biologics. The airport's strategic location in the geographic centre of peninsular India makes it an ideal transit point for traffic between Europe and Southeast Asia, and airlines like Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Singapore Airlines have significantly expanded their Hyderabad operations in recent years.

Cochin International Airport in Kerala occupies a unique position in the Indian aviation landscape. It was the first airport in the world to be fully powered by solar energy, a distinction that has made it a global symbol of sustainable aviation. But Cochin's ambitions extend far beyond environmental credentials. The airport, which is operated by Cochin International Airport Limited — a public limited company with over 300,000 individual shareholders, making it one of the most widely held companies in India — has emerged as the primary gateway for the vast Kerala diaspora in the Gulf states. Over 80% of its international traffic is to Middle Eastern destinations, and the airport has leveraged this to develop one of the most efficient transit operations in Asia, with minimum connection times of just 75 minutes. The airport's fourth terminal, currently under construction, will add 12 million passengers of capacity, while a new cargo complex will double freight handling to 200,000 tonnes annually.

Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru, India's technology capital, which has grown from a modest 7-million-passenger facility to a 40-million-passenger hub serving as the primary gateway for the Indian technology industry's global connections.

Photo: Ank Kumar, Infosys / Wikimedia Commons

The Expanding Universe: Chennai, Goa, and the Transformation of Mumbai

The southern city of Chennai, long overshadowed by Bengaluru and Hyderabad in the technology race, is mounting its own aviation challenge. Chennai International Airport is undergoing a ₹2,000-crore expansion that will see the construction of a new integrated terminal building, replacing the aging domestic and international terminals that have served the city since the 1980s. The new terminal, designed to handle 35 million passengers annually, will feature a distinctive wave-like roof inspired by the Bay of Bengal and traditional Tamil architecture. Chennai's strategic importance lies in its position as the gateway to Southeast Asia — it is closer to Singapore than any other major Indian city — and its large automotive and manufacturing base generates substantial cargo traffic. The airport's cargo complex, which handles over 400,000 tonnes annually, is being expanded with dedicated facilities for automobile components, textiles, and electronic goods.

Goa, India's most popular tourist destination, has entered a new era of aviation with the opening of Mopa International Airport in North Goa. The airport, which began operations in 2022, was designed to relieve pressure on the aging Dabolim Airport, which shared its runway with the Indian Navy's air station — a constraint that limited civilian operations to just 12 hours a day. Mopa, named after the nearby village, is a greenfield facility with a capacity of 4.4 million passengers in its first phase, expandable to 13.1 million. The airport's design, by the Indian firm GMR Goa International Airport Limited, incorporates traditional Goan architectural elements — laterite stone facades, Mangalore tile roofs, and open-air courtyards — creating a sense of place that is often missing from modern airport architecture. The airport has already attracted international carriers from Russia, the United Kingdom, and the Gulf states, and its opening has catalysed the development of North Goa as a distinct tourism and hospitality hub.

Rajiv Gandhi International Airport in Hyderabad, which has evolved from a modest facility into a major international hub handling over 25 million passengers and serving as a critical node in global pharmaceutical supply chains.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Mumbai's existing airport is not standing still while Navi Mumbai rises. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport is undergoing a comprehensive modernisation program that includes the construction of a new integrated Terminal 2, which has already added significant capacity, along with upgrades to the airport's airside infrastructure, including new taxiways and apron areas designed to reduce congestion and improve aircraft turnaround times. The airport's cargo complex, which handles over 800,000 tonnes annually, is being expanded with dedicated facilities for pharmaceutical products, gold, and precious stones — reflecting Mumbai's role as India's financial and commercial capital. The airport operator, Mumbai International Airport Limited (a joint venture between GVK and the Airports Authority of India), has also invested heavily in passenger experience improvements, including automated biometric processing, self-service bag drop, and a redesigned retail and dining precinct that showcases India's culinary diversity.

UDAN: Connecting a Nation from the Ground Up

No account of India's aviation revolution would be complete without a discussion of the UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Naagrik) scheme, the regional connectivity program that has been described as the most ambitious attempt at democratising air travel since the deregulation of the American airline industry in 1978. Launched in 2016, UDAN — which translates to "fly the common citizen" — aims to make air travel affordable and widespread by subsidising operations on underserved and unserved routes, developing new airports and heliports, and creating a network of regional air services that connects India's smaller cities and towns to the national aviation grid. The scheme has been nothing short of transformative: in its first five years, UDAN revived or created over 450 routes, connected 74 unserved or underserved airports, and carried over 10 million passengers who had never before flown.

The economic logic behind UDAN is compelling. India has over 400 airstrips and airports, but until the scheme's launch, only about 70 were served by scheduled commercial flights. The vast majority of India's 1.4 billion people lived more than 100 kilometres from an airport with regular service, effectively excluding them from the aviation economy. UDAN changed this by offering viability gap funding to airlines operating on regional routes, capping fares at ₹2,500 (approximately $30) for one-hour flights, and providing airport operators with reduced landing and parking charges on regional routes. The result has been the emergence of a new generation of regional carriers — Star Air, IndiaOne Air, FlyBig, and the regional arm of IndiGo — that operate smaller aircraft like the ATR 72 and the Dornier 228 on routes that would be economically unviable without government support.

The scheme's impact on regional economies has been profound. Cities like Jaisalmer, Kullu, and Pakyong, which were previously accessible only by long and often arduous road journeys, now have regular air connections to major cities, catalysing tourism, trade, and investment. The development of new airports in tier-2 and tier-3 cities has created thousands of direct and indirect jobs, stimulated real estate development, and improved access to healthcare and education. The government's target of operationalising 220 airports and heliports by 2026, up from 141 in 2022, represents one of the most rapid expansions of aviation infrastructure in history. UDAN has also served as a proving ground for new technologies and operational models, including seaplane services in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, helicopter connectivity in the mountainous states of the Northeast, and the use of drones for medical supply delivery in remote areas.

The Transit Revolution: Immigration, ITD, and the Art of the Connection

Building world-class terminals and runways is necessary but not sufficient to create a genuine international hub. The true test of a hub airport lies in its ability to process connecting passengers quickly, efficiently, and with minimal friction — and it is in this area that Indian airports have made perhaps their most significant strides in recent years. The introduction of the Immigration ITD (Immediate Transit Departure) facility at major Indian airports has been a game-changer for transit passengers. Under this system, passengers connecting between international flights can transit without entering India's immigration system, remaining in secure, airside transit lounges that offer a range of amenities including sleeping pods, shower facilities, business centres, and a curated selection of dining and retail options.

The ITD facility at Delhi's Terminal 3 is widely regarded as the gold standard. Spanning over 15,000 square metres, it can accommodate up to 2,000 simultaneous transit passengers and features dedicated zones for different airline alliances and destination regions. The facility is supported by a state-of-the-art baggage handling system that can transfer luggage between flights in under 45 minutes, enabling minimum connection times of just 90 minutes — competitive with the best hubs in the world. Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad have since introduced their own ITD facilities, and the government has mandated that all airports handling more than 5 million international passengers annually must have dedicated transit infrastructure by 2027.

Complementing the ITD facilities is the rapid digitisation of India's immigration and border control processes. The e-Visa system, which covers citizens of 170 countries, has been expanded to include multiple-entry and long-duration visas, while the DigiYatra biometric boarding system, which uses facial recognition technology to process passengers from check-in to boarding without the need for physical documents, has been deployed at over 20 Indian airports. The government's Immigration, Visa and Foreigners Registration and Tracking (IVFRT) system, which integrates data from airlines, immigration, and security agencies, has reduced average immigration processing times from over 45 seconds per passenger to under 15 seconds — a critical improvement for transit operations where every minute counts. The introduction of automated e-gates at Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru has further streamlined the process, with Indian citizens now able to clear immigration in under 10 seconds.

Steel and Concrete: The Rail Revolution at India's Airports

One of the most underappreciated aspects of India's airport transformation is the integration of rail connectivity — a recognition that the world's best airports are not merely aviation facilities but multimodal transport hubs that seamlessly connect air, rail, and road networks. Delhi Airport Metro Express, India's first airport rail link, has been operating since 2011, connecting the airport to New Delhi Railway Station in under 20 minutes at speeds of up to 120 kilometres per hour. The line, which was briefly suspended in 2013 due to technical issues, was revived and upgraded in 2023 with new rolling stock and signalling systems, and now carries over 25,000 passengers daily. A planned extension will connect the line to the upcoming Jewar Airport, creating a seamless rail corridor between Delhi's two airports.

Mumbai's airport rail connectivity is being transformed by the Mumbai Metro network, with Line 3 (the Colaba-Bandra-SEEPZ line) set to provide a direct underground connection to both the domestic and international terminals of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport. The line, expected to be fully operational by 2027, will reduce travel time between South Mumbai and the airport from over 90 minutes by road to just 30 minutes by metro. Navi Mumbai Airport will be served by the Navi Mumbai Metro's Line 1, with a dedicated airport station connected to the terminal via a people mover system. The Mumbai Trans-Harbour Link, India's longest sea bridge at 21.8 kilometres, will provide a high-speed road connection between the two cities, while the proposed Mumbai-Hyderabad high-speed rail corridor could eventually link the two cities' airports at speeds of up to 300 kilometres per hour.

In Bengaluru, the airport's rail connectivity has been a long-standing challenge that is finally being addressed. The Bengaluru Metro's Blue Line will include a dedicated airport station, connected to the terminal via an automated people mover, with services expected to commence by 2027. The 41-kilometre line will connect the airport to the city's eastern suburbs and the Whitefield technology corridor, home to hundreds of multinational companies. Hyderabad's airport is served by the Hyderabad Metro's Airport Express, a dedicated line that connects the terminal to the city centre in 24 minutes, while a proposed extension will link the airport to the upcoming Hyderabad-Secunderabad high-speed rail station. Cochin Airport, which currently relies on road connectivity, will be served by the Kochi Metro's extension to the airport, a 12-kilometre line that is under construction and expected to open by 2028.

The Road Network: Expressways as Airport Arteries

While rail connectivity is essential, the reality of Indian transportation is that roads remain the dominant mode of passenger and freight movement, and the government has invested heavily in expressway infrastructure linking major airports to their catchment areas. The Yamuna Expressway, a 165-kilometre, six-lane access-controlled highway connecting Greater Noida to Agra, serves as the primary road link for both Delhi's IGIA and the upcoming Jewar Airport. The Delhi-Mumbai Expressway, a 1,386-kilometre, eight-lane corridor that will reduce travel time between the two cities from 24 hours to just 12, passes within 50 kilometres of both airports and includes dedicated spur roads for airport access. The Bengaluru-Mysuru Expressway, the Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways around Delhi, and the Mumbai-Pune Expressway are all being upgraded or extended to improve airport connectivity.

The Mumbai Trans-Harbour Link, which opened to traffic in 2024, deserves special mention as a transformative piece of infrastructure. The 21.8-kilometre sea bridge, which connects Mumbai with Navi Mumbai across Thane Creek, has reduced travel time between the two cities from over 90 minutes to less than 20, effectively merging their labour markets and catchment areas. For Navi Mumbai Airport, this means that the entire population of Greater Mumbai — over 20 million people — is now within a 45-minute drive, dramatically expanding the airport's potential passenger base. The bridge, which was built at a cost of ₹17,843 crore ($2.2 billion), is expected to carry over 70,000 vehicles daily and has already catalysed a wave of real estate development in the Navi Mumbai region.

Chennai's airport connectivity is being enhanced by the Chennai Outer Ring Road, a 62-kilometre, six-lane expressway that connects the city's northern and southern suburbs while providing a high-speed corridor to the airport. The proposed Chennai-Salem Expressway, a 277-kilometre, eight-lane highway, will connect Chennai to the industrial cities of central Tamil Nadu, expanding the airport's catchment area to include a population of over 30 million. Hyderabad's Regional Ring Road, a 340-kilometre, eight-lane expressway encircling the city, will provide seamless connectivity to Rajiv Gandhi International Airport from all directions, while the proposed Hyderabad-Indore Expressway will link the airport to central India's growing industrial belt.

The Cargo Imperative: Building the Supply Chain of Tomorrow

While passenger traffic dominates the headlines, the development of cargo infrastructure is arguably the most strategically significant aspect of India's airport expansion. India's air cargo market, which handles approximately 3.5 million tonnes annually, is a fraction of the volume moved through hubs like Hong Kong (5 million tonnes), Memphis (4.5 million tonnes), and Shanghai (3.5 million tonnes in international cargo alone). But the growth trajectory is steep — air cargo has been growing at 8-10% annually, driven by the expansion of e-commerce, the pharmaceutical industry, and the relocation of global supply chains away from China. Indian airports are positioning themselves to capture a significant share of this growth, with dedicated cargo terminals, free trade zones, and multimodal logistics parks being developed across the country.

Delhi Airport's cargo complex, which handles over 1 million tonnes annually, is the largest in South Asia and is being expanded with a new integrated cargo terminal that will add 2.5 million tonnes of capacity. The facility includes dedicated cold-chain infrastructure for pharmaceutical products, hazardous materials handling, and a bonded warehouse zone that allows goods to be stored duty-free pending re-export. Mumbai's cargo operations, which handle over 800,000 tonnes annually, are being expanded with a new dedicated cargo terminal at the existing airport, while Navi Mumbai Airport's master plan includes a 1,000-acre cargo complex designed to handle 2.5 million tonnes annually. Bengaluru's cargo terminal, which handles over 400,000 tonnes, is being expanded with dedicated facilities for electronics and pharmaceutical shipments, while Hyderabad's cargo complex has become a global hub for vaccine distribution, handling over 50% of India's vaccine exports.

The government's National Logistics Policy, launched in 2022, provides the policy framework for this expansion, with a target of reducing logistics costs from 14-16% of GDP to 8% by 2030 — bringing India in line with developed economies. The policy includes provisions for dedicated air cargo corridors, simplified customs procedures, and the development of 35 multimodal logistics parks across the country, many of which will be co-located with airports. The Airports Authority of India has also introduced a cargo incentive scheme that offers reduced handling charges, priority landing slots, and streamlined customs clearance for freight operators using Indian airports as regional distribution hubs. The results are already visible: Delhi Airport has emerged as a major transshipment point for cargo moving between Europe and East Asia, while Bengaluru and Hyderabad have become critical nodes in global pharmaceutical supply chains.
